title: Health Policy, Planning and Management
description: Health systems and financing in Nigeria, policy development, health planning, management functions, and monitoring and evaluation.

topics.title: Health Systems and the Nigerian Health Sector
topics.summary: WHO building blocks, levels of care, governance and key health institutions in Nigeria.

notes.b: A health system comprises all organisations, people and actions whose primary intent is to promote, restore or maintain health. The WHO framework has six building blocks: service delivery; health workforce; health information systems; access to essential medicines, vaccines and technologies; health financing; and leadership and governance. The goals are improved health (level and equity), responsiveness, social and financial risk protection, and improved efficiency. Universal health coverage (UHC — SDG target 3.8) means all people receive quality health services they need without suffering financial hardship; its dimensions are population coverage, service coverage and financial protection (the UHC cube).
k: UHC cube: who, what services, what cost

notes.b: Nigeria's health system is organised in three tiers aligned with government levels: primary health care (PHC) under local governments (with state PHC boards under the 'PHC Under One Roof' policy), secondary care (general hospitals) under states, and tertiary care (teaching hospitals, federal medical centres) under the Federal Government. Key institutions: the Federal Ministry of Health and Social Welfare, the National Primary Health Care Development Agency (NPHCDA), the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), NAFDAC (regulating food and drugs), the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA), and professional regulatory councils (MDCN, NMCN, PCN, MLSCN, RRBN, MRTB). The National Health Act 2014 provides the legal framework and created the Basic Health Care Provision Fund (BHCPF). Challenges: underfunding, brain drain of health workers ('japa'), weak referral systems, inequitable distribution and high out-of-pocket spending.

topics.title: Health Financing
topics.summary: Sources of funding, out-of-pocket payments, health insurance and financing reforms.

notes.b: Health financing involves revenue collection (taxes, insurance contributions, out-of-pocket payments, donor funds), pooling (spreading financial risk across a population) and purchasing (paying providers — capitation, fee-for-service, diagnosis-related groups, results-based financing). Out-of-pocket (OOP) payments account for over 70% of Nigeria's health spending, among the highest in the world, causing catastrophic health expenditure (spending > 10% or 40% of capacity to pay, depending on definition) and impoverishment. The Abuja Declaration (2001) committed African governments to allocate at least 15% of their budgets to health; Nigeria allocates far less (around 5%).

The National Health Insurance Scheme (1999, operational 2005) was replaced by the National Health Insurance Authority Act 2022, which makes health insurance mandatory for all Nigerians and establishes a Vulnerable Group Fund to cover the poor. State Supported Health Insurance Schemes (e.g. Lagos LSHS, Kwara, Ekiti) extend coverage. Community-based health insurance pools resources locally. Providers under the formal sector programme are often paid by capitation (fixed amount per enrollee per period) for primary care and fee-for-service for secondary care. The Basic Health Care Provision Fund (at least 1% of the Consolidated Revenue Fund) finances a minimum package through PHCs and insurance. Results-based financing pays providers for verified outputs (e.g. deliveries, immunisations). Insurance coverage remains low (under 10% of the population).

topics.title: Health Policy Development
topics.summary: The policy process, stakeholders, the policy triangle and major Nigerian health policies.

notes.b: Health policy consists of courses of action (and inaction) by governments and organisations that affect health. The policy cycle includes agenda setting, policy formulation, adoption, implementation and evaluation. Kingdon's multiple streams model explains agenda setting: problem, policy (solutions) and politics streams converge in a 'policy window'. Walt and Gilson's policy triangle analyses context, content, process and actors (who hold power). Stakeholder analysis maps actors by interest and influence. Evidence-informed policymaking uses research syntheses and policy briefs, though politics, values and interests heavily influence outcomes.
k: Policy triangle: context, content, process, actors

notes.b: Nigeria's National Health Policy (first 1988, revised 2016) is based on primary health care. Others include the National Strategic Health Development Plan (NSHDP II 2018–2022 and successors), National Drug Policy, National Policy on Food and Nutrition, National Tuberculosis and HIV/AIDS policies, the National Immunisation Policy, the Task-Shifting and Task-Sharing Policy (allowing CHEWs and nurses to deliver specified services), the National Policy on Health Workforce Migration (2023), and the Health Sector Renewal Investment Initiative (2023), which emphasises a sector-wide approach (SWAp) aligning partners behind one plan, budget and monitoring framework. Implementation gaps are common due to funding, weak coordination and political change.

topics.title: Health Planning and Management
topics.summary: Planning cycle, management functions, leadership, human resources and supply chains.

notes.b: Health planning is the systematic process of deciding goals and the means to achieve them. Steps: situation analysis (health needs, resources — using tools like SWOT: strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats), priority setting (burden, feasibility, cost-effectiveness), setting SMART objectives (Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant, Time-bound), identifying strategies and activities, resource allocation and budgeting, implementation, and monitoring and evaluation. Tools include the logical framework (logframe — inputs, activities, outputs, outcomes, impact with indicators and assumptions), Gantt charts for scheduling, and operational (annual) plans derived from strategic (multi-year) plans.

Management functions (Fayol): planning, organising, staffing, directing (leading) and controlling (POSDCORB extends these). Leadership styles: autocratic, democratic (participative), laissez-faire, transformational (inspiring a shared vision) and situational. Human resource management covers recruitment, deployment, supervision (supportive supervision), motivation (Maslow's hierarchy, Herzberg's hygiene and motivator factors), performance appraisal and retention (rural incentives). Supply chain management ensures medicines and commodities are available: forecasting, procurement, storage, distribution and logistics management information systems; stock-outs are common in Nigerian PHCs. Quality improvement uses PDSA (Plan–Do–Study–Act) cycles.

topics.title: Monitoring, Evaluation and Health Information
topics.summary: M&E frameworks, indicators, DHIS2, and evaluation designs.

notes.b: Monitoring is the routine, continuous tracking of programme inputs, activities and outputs; evaluation is the periodic assessment of outcomes and impact, relevance, efficiency, effectiveness and sustainability (OECD-DAC criteria). Indicators should be valid, reliable, specific, sensitive and feasible. Types: input (e.g. number of health workers), process (e.g. training sessions held), output (e.g. number vaccinated), outcome (e.g. immunisation coverage) and impact (e.g. reduction in child mortality). Evaluation types: formative (improving a programme during implementation), process, outcome and impact evaluation. Designs range from before–after comparisons to randomised trials; baseline data are essential.

Nigeria's National Health Management Information System (NHMIS) collects routine facility data using standard registers and monthly summary forms, entered into DHIS2 (District Health Information Software 2). Other sources: population census, civil registration and vital statistics (weak — many births and deaths unregistered), surveys (Nigeria Demographic and Health Survey — NDHS, Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey — MICS), disease surveillance (IDSR — Integrated Disease Surveillance and Response) and research. Data quality dimensions: completeness, timeliness, accuracy and consistency. Data should be used for decision-making at all levels, not just reported upwards.
